title: Add the Last Three
statement:
The **tribonacci** numbers are defined by `T(0) = 0`, `T(1) = 1`, `T(2) = 1` and, for `n >= 3`, `T(n) = T(n - 1) + T(n - 2) + T(n - 3)` (each number is the sum of the three before it: 0, 1, 1, 2, 4, 7, 13, ...).

Return `T(n)`.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 37 (the answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer)

hints.nudge: The definition is a recursion. Is the plain recursive function fast enough for n = 37? Count how often it computes the same value.
hints.pattern: Compute the numbers in order from T(0) upwards and keep only the last three values (a loop instead of a recursion), or memoise the recursion.
hints.pseudocode:
a = 0; b = 1; c = 1
for i in 3 .. n: next = a + b + c; a = b; b = c; c = next
return the right value for n < 3 (0, 1, 1), otherwise c
hints.walkthrough: The direct recursion T(n) = T(n - 1) + T(n - 2) + T(n - 3) calls itself three times, so the number of calls grows exponentially (billions of calls for n = 37). Each value only depends on the three values before it, so compute them from the bottom: keep the three latest values in variables a, b, c, and in each step replace them by (b, c, a + b + c). The loop runs n - 3 times: O(n) time and O(1) memory. The largest case, T(37) = 2,082,876,103, fits in a 32-bit integer.
